concepts.name: Map identity equality and insertion order

questions.prompt: A Map stores a value under `{id:1}`. Looking it up with a different newly created `{id:1}` fails. Why?

choices.text: Object keys use identity rather than equality of their visible fields.
Map keys use JSON equality but only after values are sorted alphabetically.
Map supports object keys only when those objects were explicitly frozen.
Map converts both object keys to strings and rejects their repeated spelling.

questions.explanation: Separate object instances are distinct keys even when fields look the same. Map does not stringify keys or compare their JSON structure.

sources.title: ECMAScript: Keyed Collections
sources.claim: Map preserves insertion order and uses SameValueZero equality; weak collections do not keep keys alive or expose key enumeration.

questions.prompt: What is `new Set([NaN, NaN, 0, -0]).size` under standard equality?

choices.text: 4, because every position in the input creates a separate Set entry.
3, because NaN repeats but signed zeros remain different Set entries.
1, because Set converts all numeric keys into the same falsy entry.
2, because NaN repeats and signed zeros share the same key value.

questions.explanation: Set uses SameValueZero equality: NaN equals NaN for membership, and +0 and -0 are equivalent. Two unique values remain.

questions.prompt: A cache uses a WeakMap keyed by objects. Which feature is intentionally unavailable?

choices.text: Deleting an entry when the caller still holds its object key.
Associating a value with an accepted object key held by the caller.
Enumerating every stored key to inspect which keys are still alive.
Looking up the cached value when the caller still holds its key.

questions.explanation: WeakMap does not expose key enumeration because it would reveal collection-dependent liveness. Lookup, deletion and set with held keys are supported.

questions.prompt: `const a=[{n:1}]; const b=a.slice(); b[0].n=2;` What does a[0].n become?

choices.text: A TypeError, because copying an array makes every nested element readonly.
2, because slice copies the element reference rather than cloning its object.
1, because slice deeply clones each nested object it encounters.
undefined, because editing b removes the corresponding entry from a.

questions.explanation: Slice creates a new outer array with the same element references. A nested object mutation is visible through either array.

sources.title: ECMAScript: Indexed Collections
sources.claim: Array methods have defined mutation and comparison semantics; sorting without a comparator uses string ordering and copies can be shallow.

questions.prompt: A Map inserts a then b, updates the value for a without deleting it, and iterates keys. What key order remains?

choices.text: a then b, because updating an existing key does not reinsert it.
b then a, because every set moves its key to the end of iteration.
Alphabetical order, because Maps sort keys before iteration.
Unspecified order, because Map never preserves insertion order.

questions.explanation: Map preserves insertion order. Updating an existing entry keeps its position; delete followed by reinsert would differ.

questions.prompt: A Set contains one object. Adding the same object reference again has what effect on size?

choices.text: It increases by one because object references never participate in equality.
It doubles because Set clones objects when inserting them.
It becomes zero because adding a duplicate clears the collection.
It stays unchanged because the existing key is already present.

questions.explanation: Set membership uses key equality, including object identity. Inserting the same object again does not create a second entry.

questions.prompt: A Map serves as an object-keyed lookup table. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Iteration preserves insertion order.
Updating an existing key moves it to the end automatically.
Map compares every object key by JSON serialization.
Deleting then reinserting a key can change its position.
Different object instances can be different keys with identical fields.

questions.explanation: a: Entries are iterated in their insertion sequence. b: The existing entry retains its position. c: It compares object identity instead. d: Reinsertion creates a new entry at the end. e: Object key identity is not structural equality.

questions.prompt: A deduplication step uses Set. Which equality claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Two objects with equal fields must share one entry.
The same object reference can occupy multiple unique entries.
Set sorts numeric values before exposing iteration.
Repeated NaN values share one entry.
Positive and negative zero share one entry.

questions.explanation: a: Different object identities remain distinct. b: Repeated insertion of the same key does not add an entry. c: It preserves insertion order rather than numeric sorting. d: SameValueZero treats NaN as equivalent for membership. e: SameValueZero does not distinguish signed zeros.

questions.prompt: A WeakMap supports a cache keyed by objects. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: It guarantees removal at the next timer tick after a reference is dropped.
It provides a size counter that is updated synchronously by garbage collection.
Its entries do not keep otherwise unreachable keys alive.
Holding a key allows lookup of its associated value.
It intentionally omits general key enumeration.

questions.explanation: a: Collection timing is not guaranteed that way. b: WeakMap does not expose a size counter. c: Weak keys are not strong reachability roots. d: get is supported when the caller supplies the key. e: Enumeration would expose collection-dependent liveness.

questions.prompt: An array slice is used before editing object records. Which copy claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Reassigning one new-array slot necessarily changes the original slot.
The new outer array can be changed independently.
Nested object references can still be shared.
Mutating a shared nested object can affect both views.
slice automatically deep-clones all reachable records.

questions.explanation: a: The separate outer arrays have separate element slots. b: Slice returns a distinct array container. c: Element references are copied rather than deeply cloned. d: Both arrays may reference that same object. e: It is a shallow copy operation.
